topic: bark tanning a heavy cowhide: pit liquors, substance through the butt and dressing the dried leather

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: cyfrowy grubosciomierz na warsztacie

base: I am bark tanning a heavy cowhide in pits behind the shed and progress seems slow.
A calf skin went into the weakest pit at the same time and has coloured right through.
A digital thickness gauge lives on the bench and I read each hide in three places.
The cowhide still shows a pale streak down the middle when I cut a test corner.
Should I move it to a stronger liquor, or simply leave it where it is?
Leave it, because a stronger liquor now will case harden the outside and seal the middle.
Thick hides must start weak and climb slowly, over months rather than weeks.
The pale streak simply means the tan has not yet reached the centre of the substance.
Handle the hide every few days so fresh liquor reaches the folds and the belly.
I have handled it twice a week and moved it up through three stronger pits.
The thickness gauge shows four millimetres at the butt and barely two at the flank.
The calf skin came out weeks ago and has already been oiled and hung to dry.
Does the thin flank finish long before the butt, and will it suffer for that?
The flank does finish first, though it takes no harm from the extra time in liquor.
Vegetable tan fills a hide rather than burning it, so weeks of overlap are harmless.
Judge the butt by cutting a corner and looking for an even colour right through.
A pale core at four millimetres usually wants another two months in the strongest pit.
Two more months have passed and the test corner now shows one even brown colour.
I lifted the hide out, rinsed it briefly and hung it in the loft to drain.
The thickness gauge now reads a shade under four at the butt, which surprised me.
Should I oil it wet, or wait until the hide has dried to the touch?
Oil it while it is still damp, at about the stage the leather feels cool but not wet.
Dry leather will not take the dubbin and you end up with a greasy surface only.
Work the mixture in warm, a little at a time, and give the flesh side most.
The calf skin will have taken far less, since thin leather needs only a light dressing.
I dressed it damp with warm tallow and cod oil and the hide drank it steadily.
After a week the surface feels supple, though one shoulder has stayed noticeably stiffer.
That shoulder is also the part that hung nearest the loft window in the sun.
Can a stiff shoulder be brought back, or has the sun spoiled it for good?
It can usually be brought back, provided the leather never grew hot to the hand.
Damp that shoulder with a sponge, let it stand overnight and dress it a second time.
Then work it over a stake, drawing the flesh side across the edge again and again.
Sun struck leather that has gone hard and horny will not answer to any of this.
The shoulder softened after a second dressing and an hour of staking on the beam.
The whole hide now bends without cracking and shows a close, even grain throughout.
I would like to start another hide in autumn and run the pits through the winter.
Does cold weather slow the tanning badly, or can the pits work all year round?
Cold slows it a great deal, and below five degrees the liquor works hardly at all.
Old yards started hides in autumn all the same, accepting that winter was a resting time.
Keep the pits covered and topped up, since frost on the surface does real harm.
Then count on the work waking again in March and finishing by the following autumn.
